about: Party positions on 30 statements, coded independently by two coders from published sources (manifesto first, then votes, questionnaire answers, dated statements, coalition actions) and reconciled by a third reviewer. Evidence, URL, tier and confidence are published for every cell. See guide/quiz-method.md and raw/quiz2/RECONCILIATION.md.

evidence_tiers.1: party's 2026 manifesto / policy document / policy page
evidence_tiers.2: recorded party vote in the 54th Parliament on legislation enacting or repealing the proposal

statements.text: The government should take active steps to reduce the gap between high and low incomes, even if that means higher taxes for some people.

national.evidence: Coder A: National's 2026 'no new taxes' pledge (23 Aug 2026) rules out any new tax including wealth or capital taxes; Fiscal Plan commits to reducing Crown spending toward 30% of GDP (9 Aug 2026). Willis: 'We will not introduce a capital gains tax' (28 Oct 2025). No redistribution-through-tax commitment anywhere in 2026 material. Coder B: No 2026 text on narrowing the income gap; National's fiscal plan rules out 'new taxes' and attacks Labour/Greens/TPM 'nine new taxes' as punishing 'Kiwis who do the right thing and save and invest' (Fiscal Plan, Oct 2026). Inference from explicit general principle (no higher taxes) -> disagree; recorded as inference. Reconciler: Both coders derive the value from the same 'no new taxes' pledge; neither found any 2026 text on narrowing the income gap. That is the permitted inference from an explicit general principle, which section 4.1(3) caps at +/-1 with low confidence. A's -2 (high) is reduced accordingly.

labour.evidence: Labour's 2026 platform introduces a 28% CGT on investment and commercial property (announced 28 Oct 2025, applies from 1 Jul 2027), ring-fenced to fund free GP visits and other health spending; it also commits to higher minimum wages and restoring pay equity. Redistribution is a theme but the tax is narrow and the family home, farms, shares and business assets are exempt, so support is qualified.

green.evidence: 2026 tax policy 'A tax system for all of us' (21 Jun 2026): 2.5% wealth tax on net assets over $10m, capital acquisitions tax on large gifts/inheritances, 45% rate above $160,000, higher corporate taxes, funding a $10,000 tax-free threshold and income tax cuts for 96% of earners. Grey Power response: tax policy 'will redistribute wealth'.

act.evidence: Coder A: ACT 2026 Fiscal Plan cuts non-frontline spending to 2017 levels per person and 'pays down debt faster'; ACT 'strongly opposes any new tax, because once they're in, they always grow' (Free Press, 17 Aug 2026); Seymour on Labour's CGT: 'Another tax is not the solution to our problems' (28 Oct 2025). Coder B: Fiscal Plan 2026 cuts spending to 2017 per-person levels and rules out new taxes; Seymour (CA ANZ forum, 21 Sep 2026): the problem is public-sector productivity, 'not too little revenue'; ACT campaigns against wealth/asset taxes as 'envy taxes'. Emphasised rejection of higher taxes for redistribution.

nz-first.evidence: Coder A: NZ First would cut the company tax rate to 20% for firms under $30m turnover (24 Sep 2026) and increase the In-Work Tax Credit by $70/week funded from existing spending; Peters called Labour's CGT 'an absolute mess of an announcement' (28 Oct 2025). Supports some redistribution (WFF, minimum wage) but opposes higher taxes to pay for it. Coder B: Peters attacks 'neoliberal' asset sales and wants a state bank, higher minimum wage with inflation and a $70 In-Work Tax Credit rise, but also calls TOP's/Greens' wealth taxes 'communism' (13 Sep 2026) and proposes a 20% SME tax rate. Both sides emphasised -> argued neutral. Reconciler: A (-1) and B (0) document the same two facts: NZ First proposes redistribution (In-Work Tax Credit rise, minimum-wage indexation, state bank) and simultaneously rejects higher taxes (SME tax cut; wealth taxes called 'communism', 13 Sep 2026). The statement is a trade-off and the party emphasises both sides without choosing: EUvox argued-neutral case 2. Consistent with its E2 and E7 codings.

te-pati-maori.evidence: 'A Kiwi Tax Plan' (Aug 2026): first $30,000 tax-free, six bands with a 48% top rate above $300,000, tiered wealth tax from 1.5% on net wealth over $2m, 5% stamp duty; explicitly aimed at shifting the tax burden from low earners to the wealthy.

opportunity.evidence: Tax Reset: 1.75% land value tax and three income tax rates (28/34/39%) funding a universal Citizens' Income of up to $370/week and Child Support Incomes; designed to lift low incomes while taxing land wealth, though the party frames it as a 'reset' rather than a redistributive tax rise.

animal-justice.evidence: People policies address 'economic inequality' and reducing inequality through employment law and transition support; no tax policy stated. Qualified, low. Reconciler: Explicit commitment to reduce economic inequality through employment law and transition support; no tax measure. Partial: +1 low.

alliance.evidence: Alliance Tax Justice policy (Sep 2026): first $20,000 tax-free, upper rates of 34/39/47%, a 2.5% annual wealth tax on net wealth over $2m, a 33% CGT and a financial transactions levy, explicitly to shift tax from wages onto wealth; party describes itself as democratic socialist.

conservative.evidence: Coder A: Conservative economy policy: cut personal and company tax, align the company rate with the top personal rate, lower GST to 12.5%, and a 2025 release calls for a flat tax; 'We support lower taxes, responsible spending' (2026 site). Coder B: Finance policy: 'press for a flat tax rate for individuals and for companies'; principles: New Zealanders 'free to enjoy the fruits of their labour to the greatest possible extent'. Explicit principle against redistributive taxation; qualified. Reconciler: Flat tax and lower taxes are explicit and emphasised, but the party says nothing about the income gap itself; the value is an inference from an explicit tax principle, so -1 under section 4.1(3). Confidence medium because the flat-tax commitment is a direct rejection of progressive taxation.

womens-rights.evidence: 'Minimum wages and benefits need to be increased so that all people have living incomes'; CPAG-style Working for Families reform for 'the poorest families'. No tax measure; qualified, low. Reconciler: Explicit: raise minimum wages and benefits 'so that all people have living incomes' and target Working for Families at the poorest. Direction explicit, tax side unaddressed: +1 low.

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: Universal Whānau Allowance, debt amnesty, 25% mana whenua equity in regional infrastructure, living-wage trade academy - redistribution without a stated tax measure; qualified, low. Reconciler: Universal Whānau Allowance, debt amnesty and mana whenua equity stakes are explicit redistribution; no tax measure: +1 low.

statements.text: Lower taxes do more good for New Zealand than more government spending, even if it means fewer public services.

national.evidence: Coder A: National: 'keep taxes low', no new taxes, reduce Crown expenditure toward 30% of GDP, return to surplus by 2028/29 (Aug 2026); but also funds Pharmac, school lunches, paid parental leave extensions, so 'fewer public services' is not embraced. Supports the direction with qualifications. Coder B: Fiscal Plan (Oct 2026): 'not impose new taxes', 'show ongoing restraint so that overall government expenditure comes down towards 30% of GDP', 'right-sizing government'; but also pledges to 'continue investing in health, schools, law and order' - so a qualified preference for lower tax/smaller state.

labour.evidence: Coder A: Labour would raise a CGT to fund Medicard free GP visits, free prescriptions and other services; targets core Crown spending and revenue of about 33% of GDP (higher than National's 30%) and would reverse planned public service cuts (Fiscal Plan). Prefers service spending over tax cuts. Coder B: Fiscal Strategy 2026: 'balance the books without shrinking the economy'; funds Medicard, free prescriptions and public-service restoration partly through a new CGT; attacks National's tax cuts 'to those at the top'. Prefers services over tax cuts, qualified.

green.evidence: Coder A: Greens' 2026 manifesto: 'Fund public services adequately', Green Budget 2025 expands health, education, income support funded by wealth and corporate taxes; tax policy raises net revenue from the super-rich to pay for services. Coder B: Greens fund free ECE, dental, fees-free and public housing by taxing 'the super-rich and large corporates'; manifesto: 'fund public services adequately'; Green Budget 2025 raises revenue and borrowing rather than cutting.

act.evidence: Fiscal Plan 2026: 'reducing spending to 2017 levels adjusted for wages, inflation and population', cut new spending from $2.4b to $2b, consolidate 43 departments to 19; balancethebooks.nz: 'ACT will pay down debt faster'; tax cuts funded from smaller government.

nz-first.evidence: NZ First proposes both tax cuts (20% company rate for SMEs) and large new spending (a $100bn Future Fund for infrastructure, $5,000-a-year Kiwi Kids Grant, higher WFF, universal Super protected). Argued neutral: both sides emphasised, no stated preference for lower taxes over services. Reconciler: Tax cuts (20% SME rate) and very large new spending ($100bn Future Fund, Kiwi Kids Grant) proposed together with no stated preference: both sides emphasised, argued neutral. Consistent with E1 and E7.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Kiwi Tax Plan raises revenue from wealth and high incomes to fund doubled baseline benefits, a $4.5bn Oranga Whenua Oranga Tangata Fund, Māori health/education/justice authorities; the policy tool prioritises public spending over tax cuts.

opportunity.evidence: Coder A: Opportunity's Tax Reset is revenue-shifting (land value tax to fund a Citizens' Income) and it proposes a $60bn Infrastructure Fund, a 10-year health plan with 'predictable increases to baselines' and restored polytechnic funding (Grey Power response, 2026). Does not favour lower taxes at the expense of services. Coder B: Tax Reset shifts tax onto land to fund a universal income and keeps revenue; infrastructure policy to borrow for $60b of investment; 10-year health plan lifting funding to 9% of GDP. Opposes smaller-state framing; qualified.

nz-outdoors-freedom.evidence: 'Smaller, leaner central government', 'Ending Bureaucratic Waste', shrink central ministries; no tax-cut pledge. Qualified, low. Reconciler: 'Smaller, leaner central government', shrink ministries and 'end bureaucratic waste' is an explicit general principle whose scope plainly covers preferring a smaller state to more services: +1 low.

alliance.evidence: Alliance: free GP, dental, optical and audiology care, universal benefits, free public transport, 52 weeks paid parental leave, funded by wealth, capital gains and higher income taxes (Tax Justice policy, Sep 2026).

conservative.evidence: Coder A: 'We support lower taxes, responsible spending and fewer unnecessary regulations'; cut personal, company tax and GST; health 'the key issue is whether patients are treated in time, not how much is spent' (2026 site). Coder B: Small Government page: 'over-governed, over-regulated, and over-taxed'; 'Government spending and borrowing... must be slashed'; cut personal and company tax, GST to 12.5%; 'shrink government so that it focuses on its core business'.

statements.text: Gains people make from rising property and asset values should be taxed in the same way as income from work.

national.evidence: Coder A: Nicola Willis, 28 Oct 2025: National 'will not introduce a capital gains tax', calling Labour's plan 'an attack on investment and savings'; Luxon: 'a tax on every single business'. 2026 'no new taxes' pledge (23 Aug 2026) rules out any new tax. Coder B: 'No new taxes, including no capital gains tax' (Fiscal Plan, Oct 2026); Luxon 21 Jun 2026: 'not smashing ambition with a Capital Gains Tax'; 'New Zealand's lack of a capital gains tax is a real competitive advantage' (23 Aug 2026).

labour.evidence: Labour's 2026 CGT: a flat 28% on gains from residential investment and commercial property only, excluding the family home, farms, KiwiSaver, shares, business assets and inheritances (announced 28 Oct 2025). Supports taxing some asset gains, but at a flat rate on a narrow base rather than 'in the same way as income from work'.

green.evidence: Coder A: Greens' 2026 tax policy taxes wealth directly (2.5% on net assets over $10m), taxes large gifts and inheritances, and restores a 10-year bright-line test and removes interest deductibility; Swarbrick called Labour's property-only CGT 'watered down' and 'far short' (28 Oct 2025). Clear, emphasised support for taxing asset wealth and gains. Coder B: Standing economic policy: 'expanding the progressive tax system to equitably tax wealth and all forms of income, such as through capital gains, land, wealth, and inheritance taxes'; 2026 wealth tax and capital acquisitions tax; criticised Labour's CGT as too limited.

act.evidence: Coder A: Seymour on Labour's CGT: 'Another tax is not the solution to our problems' (28 Oct 2025); ACT policies cut tax on capital (no tax on KiwiSaver earnings; landlords may offset rental losses, 'abolish another of Labour's renters' taxes'). Coder B: KPMG 2026 tracker records ACT: 'No capital gains tax', 'No wealth tax/inheritance tax', tax exemption for crypto gains held over a year; ACT releases attack Labour's 'capital gains caucus' (2026). Consistent long-standing opposition.

nz-first.evidence: Coder A: Peters called Labour's CGT 'an absolute mess of an announcement' (28 Oct 2025); NZ First vetoed a CGT in 2019 ('would not budge') and has never supported a broad capital gains tax. No 2026 policy to tax capital gains. Coder B: KPMG 2026 tracker: NZ First 'Not stated' on CGT and 'Not stated, has previously opposed such taxes' on wealth tax; Peters 13 Sep 2026 derides TOP's land tax and Green asset taxes. Inference from explicit rejection of wealth/land taxes; low. Reconciler: Peters' derision of Labour's CGT (Oct 2025) and of wealth/land taxes (Sep 2026) is explicit opposition, but there is no 2026 policy document and KPMG's tracker records 'not stated'. -2 requires an emphasised, unconditional position; -1 fits.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Kiwi Tax Plan: wealth tax on net assets, 2% vacant house tax, land-banking tax, 5% stamp duty, repeal landlord interest deductibility; taxes asset holdings rather than realised gains like income - partial match. Reconciler: The Kiwi Tax Plan (Aug 2026) taxes net wealth, vacant houses, land-banking and residential sales (stamp duty) but contains no capital gains tax: the archived plan never mentions capital gains. The statement is about taxing gains like income; taxing asset holdings is a partial match, so +1 (B's reading).

opportunity.evidence: Tax Reset: 1.75% annual land value tax (0.5% rural) because 'work is heavily taxed while untaxed capital gains on housing enrich property owners'. Taxes land wealth annually rather than realised gains as income, so partial support.

alliance.evidence: Alliance Tax Justice policy: 33% capital gains tax on realised gains (excluding the family home) covering investment property, shares and business assets, plus a 2.5% wealth tax over $2m (Sep 2026).

statements.text: Services like electricity, housing and transport are delivered better by private businesses competing than by government ownership.

national.evidence: Luxon has called for a 'mature conversation' about selling assets the Crown has no reason to hold and asset recycling after the 2026 election (Nov 2025; reported Aug 2026); National's Electrify NZ keeps generation market-based with consistent transmission pricing for public and private players, and it uses PPPs/private finance in infrastructure. No sales this term; support for private delivery is qualified.

labour.evidence: Coder A: Labour: NZ Future Fund built on existing government assets 'keeping our assets in Kiwi hands' (10 Nov 2025); Hipkins says Labour is not considering asset sales beyond day-to-day housing churn and that under National-ACT 'there won't be anything left to sell'. Opposes privatisation but does not propose renationalisation. Coder B: NZ Future Fund: seeded state assets 'cannot be sold and will remain in public ownership for generations'; retain NZ ownership of Kiwibank; Hipkins on asset sales: 'there won't be anything left to sell'. Opposes privatisation; not an explicit claim that state delivery is better.

green.evidence: Coder A: Greens would create Kiwipower, a publicly owned electricity firming company (20 Jul 2026), bring 120 supermarket stores into public ownership, build thousands of Kāinga Ora homes and ensure 'public services (and state-owned enterprises) remain in public hands' (manifesto 2026, public services). Coder B: Kiwipower publicly owned electricity firm ('Public ownership'), KiwiMart public supermarket, 'tens of thousands of new public homes', replace Public Transport Operating Model so services are 'provided publicly instead of for profit'; public services and SOEs to 'remain in public hands'.

act.evidence: Coder A: Seymour, 24 Jan 2025: government is 'hopeless at owning things', pushed privatisation and selling Landcorp; ACT proposes public-private partnerships for cancer centres and opposes forced break-ups of gentailers (2026). Long-standing emphasised position. Coder B: Electricity policy 2026: 'Open transmission to private investment'; opposes forced break-up of gentailers; cancer centres via public-private partnerships and private capital; charter schools to 10,000 places; Seymour urged a 'principle' on selling Air New Zealand (2025).

nz-first.evidence: Coder A: 'No government with New Zealand First will be selling our assets' (Peters, 17 May 2026); NZ First would buy BNZ back into NZ ownership, break up the gentailers and 'stop this economic privatisation madness' (State of the Nation, 22 Mar 2026). Coder B: 'Backing a New Zealand owned bank': buy back BNZ as a large state-owned bank; break up the gentailers; Peters condemns parties that 'sell our assets, privatise our country' and reports of Kiwibank/Air NZ sales (17 May 2026); 'no asset sales'.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Coder A: TPM rejects privatisation and trading of water rights (Freshwater chapter 2026), proposes a $1bn Māori energy sovereignty fund and stronger regulator powers over power prices, and 'we want cheaper power and we want our people to own it'. Coder B: Freshwater policy: 'Reject privatisation and trading of water rights'; energy sovereignty plan with stronger Commerce Commission/Electricity Authority powers over prices; 2,000 papakāinga and half of new social housing for whānau Māori. Opposes privatisation; not a general ownership doctrine. Reconciler: Explicit rejection of privatising water rights and a Māori energy-ownership fund, but no general position on private versus public delivery across electricity, housing and transport. Equal evidence and tier; nearer-zero rule gives -1.

opportunity.evidence: Abundant Energy: ring-fence Crown gentailer dividends and restructure the market for competition; supports Kāinga Ora plus community providers; free public transport publicly funded. Both competition and public ownership emphasised -> argued neutral. Other coder: Opportunity would retain Crown stakes in the gentailers and use the money to fund 30GW of renewables, consolidate lines companies from 29 to fewer public/community entities, and expand Kāinga Ora and community housing; no privatisation proposed (Abundant Energy policy). Reconciler: Abundant Energy keeps Crown stakes in the gentailers and restructures the market for competition; housing policy backs both Kāinga Ora and community providers. Both sides stated by design: argued neutral (B, medium).

nz-outdoors-freedom.evidence: Fisheries policy: marine resources 'owned by the people of New Zealand... cannot become the private property of corporations'; housing policy uses 'a mixture of public and private housing model' and a hands-on Ministry of Housing. Favours public ownership of resources, mixed on services.

alliance.evidence: Public Ownership policy (Oct 2026): 're-integrate electricity generation, transmission, distribution, and retail under public ownership'; return ports, water, telecoms and Air NZ to full public ownership; 100% publicly owned transport system; state-house rebuilding.

conservative.evidence: Coder A: Mixed: health policy would 'buy private capacity where it is quicker and competitive'; natural resources policy proposes a Norway-style public-private resource JV but also state-bought oil tankers and new refineries. No general position on public v private delivery; argued neutral. Coder B: Mixed: 'the private sector prevailing over State control' and buying private hospital capacity, but also a state oil-tanker fleet, new state-backed refineries and a Norway-style public resource venture. Both sides -> argued neutral.

statements.text: People receiving benefits should face firm obligations and penalties for not meeting them, even if some households end up with less.

national.evidence: 'A firm, fair and affordable welfare system' (Oct 2026): lower Jobseeker rate after 2 of 3 years on benefit, drug testing with sanctions for non-compliance, 26-week stand-down for repeated voluntary unemployment; expanded Traffic Light sanctions in government (Social Security Amendment Act 2025).

labour.evidence: Coder A: Hipkins said the Traffic Light sanctions regime would 'continue to push people into poverty' and Sepuloni called it unfair and out of touch (Feb 2024); Labour has not announced a 2026 welfare policy to repeal sanctions. Opposes the current firm-sanctions direction. Coder B: Labour opposed the coalition's expansion of benefit sanctions (Social Security Amendment Act 2025, Traffic Light sanctions) and National's Oct 2026 welfare package; Labour did keep obligations/sanctions when in government. Coder could not retrieve the division record - verify.

green.evidence: Manifesto 2026: 'Increase benefits to liveable rates, individualise benefit entitlements and abolish benefit sanctions'; high-trust model at Work and Income; voted against Social Security Amendment Act 2025.

act.evidence: Coder A: ACT welfare policy: automatic electronic money-management cards after 4 months on Jobseeker, MSD-designated doctors for health benefits, 'a hand up not a way of life'; welcomed the 2025 Social Security Amendment Act's new sanctions. Coder B: ACT welcomed the Social Security Amendment Act 2025 ('tackle benefit dependency and restore accountability'); 2026 policy: monitor spending of jobseekers on benefit over 4 months, restrict medical certification for health benefits.

nz-first.evidence: Coder A: NZ First voted with the coalition for the Social Security Amendment Act 2025 (expanded Traffic Light sanctions) and supports a 10-year benefit stand-down for migrants; it has no standalone 2026 sanctions policy. Coalition action, flagged. Coder B: Voted for the Social Security Amendment Act 2025 (Traffic Light sanctions) as a coalition party; Peters' 2026 speeches stress 'hard work' and attack welfare dependency; no 2026 welfare manifesto found. Coalition vote, flagged.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Policy tool (2026 manifesto): double baseline benefits, 'remove sanctions and work-test obligations', cancel benefit debt owed to the Crown.

opportunity.evidence: Tax Reset replaces most benefits with a universal, unconditional Citizens' Income of up to $370/week plus fixed top-ups, removing work-test conditionality from the base payment; also opposes sub-minimum wages for disabled people.

alliance.evidence: Welfare policy (Sep 2026): a Universal Benefit, 'abolish benefit sanctions, stand-downs and beneficiary debt'; 'welfare should provide security, not punishment'.

conservative.evidence: Policy index: 'Welfare: Reform is needed. Fifty years of expanding welfare has undermined our families and created an underclass'; 'Less dependency'. No specific sanctions policy; qualified. Reconciler: 'Welfare: reform is needed. Fifty years of expanding welfare has undermined our families and created an underclass' and 'less dependency' (verified) is an explicit general welfare-reform principle whose scope covers firmer obligations; no sanctions detail: +1 low.

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: TTP would replace the benefit system with a simplified Universal Whānau Allowance for people in training or caregiving and end 'relentless' MSD penalties, with a $2bn debt amnesty.

national.evidence: Coder A: National repealed the Fair Pay Agreements Act (all MPs voted for repeal, 14 Dec 2023); NZCTU scorecard records National 'No' to restoring FPAs (National declined to answer; stance from record); 2026 small-business plan raises the threshold to initiate collective bargaining (10 employees or 20%). Coder B: Repealed Fair Pay Agreements Act Dec 2023 (all National MPs voted for repeal; NZCTU scorecard Oct 2026 records National 'No' to restoring FPAs); 2026 small-business plan would require minimum employee support before collective bargaining can start.

labour.evidence: 'Fair Pay Agreements legislation introduced in the first 100 days'; 'Collective agreements the default' (Fairer Workplaces, 2026); NZCTU scorecard: Labour 'Yes' to restoring FPAs.

green.evidence: Default union membership for new workers, expanded right to strike, reverse pay-equity and Fair Pay Agreement changes (manifesto 2026); NZCTU scorecard 'Yes' to restoring FPAs.

act.evidence: Led repeal of Fair Pay Agreements (Dec 2023); 2026 small-business policy: freeze minimum wage, 'make unions collect their own fees', protect employers from personal grievances; opposes default union membership; NZCTU 'No'.

nz-first.evidence: NZCTU scorecard Oct 2026: NZ First answered 'No' to restoring Fair Pay Agreements, 'No' to opt-out union membership, 'Yes' to minimum wage above inflation; Peters: unions represent 'left wing elitist political agendas' (22 Mar 2026). Voted for FPA repeal 2023.

te-pati-maori.evidence: NZCTU scorecard (Oct 2026): Te Pāti Māori 'Yes' to restoring FPAs in the first 100 days, 'Yes' to opt-out union membership; policy tool lifts the minimum wage to the living wage.

opportunity.evidence: NZCTU scorecard Oct 2026: Opportunity answered 'No' to restoring Fair Pay Agreements and 'No policy' on opt-out union membership (but 'Yes' to restoring pay equity, 90-day trial abolition, living wage).

animal-justice.evidence: People policies: 'Strong unions and worker rights provide the foundation for reducing inequality'; worker rights 'through collective organisation'. No FPA/industry-bargaining specifics; qualified. Reconciler: 'Strong unions and worker rights provide the foundation for reducing inequality' and rights 'through collective organisation' is an explicit principle covering union bargaining; no industry-wide bargaining specifics: +1, medium as coded.

alliance.evidence: Workers' Rights policy (Sep 2026): 'restore national collective bargaining', a broad right to strike, Work Councils in firms over 50 staff; NZCTU scorecard 'Yes' to FPAs and opt-out union membership.

womens-rights.evidence: WRP pay equity policy: 'reinstatement of legislative support for Fair Pay Agreements' alongside pay equity in public and private sectors.

statements.text: Keeping government debt low should take priority over spending more on health and education right now.

National also commits new health and education spending, so debt priority is qualified.

labour.evidence: Coder A: Labour targets net debt around 20% of GDP 'over time' and surplus by 2029/30 but would reverse half of planned public service cuts, fund Medicard, free prescriptions and nurse jobs now ('National cuts health, Labour protects it', Grey Power response 2026). Services now take priority over faster debt reduction. Coder B: Fiscal Strategy: surplus by 2029/30 and net debt 'around 20% of GDP over time', but 'You can't cut your way to growth'; prioritises Medicard, hospital repairs and school upgrades now. Qualified disagree.

green.evidence: Coder A: Greens: 'Reform the public finance system' away from debt-focused fiscal rules toward resilience and wellbeing; Green Budget 2025 and 2026 manifesto expand health, education and income support funded by new taxes. Coder B: Standing policy: 'Enabling greater government borrowing for investing in infrastructure'; manifesto reforms public finance to 'support long-term resilience... health and well-being'; Green Budget 2025 funded by taxes on wealth, not spending restraint.

act.evidence: Coder A: ACT Fiscal Plan 2026 ('ACT will pay down debt faster'): cut operating allowances to $2bn, non-frontline spending to 2017 levels, keep NZ Super Fund contributions suspended, raise the Super age to 67. Coder B: balancethebooks.nz / Fiscal Plan 2026: 'ACT will pay down debt faster', reduce operating allowance, keep NZ Super Fund contributions suspended, raise super age to 67; spending to 2017 levels.

nz-first.evidence: Coder A: NZ First attacks Labour's 'massive debt' yet proposes a $100bn borrowed Future Fund, a $5,000-a-year Kiwi Kids Grant and ring-fenced Super; no stated trade-off between debt and health/education spending. Argued neutral. te-pati-maori.evidence: Manifesto 2026 commits to large new spending (doubled benefits, free GP and dental, $4.5b Oranga Whenua fund, $1.25b kura property) funded by new taxes; no debt target; Peters criticises its scale. Spending prioritised over debt.

opportunity.evidence: Intergenerational Infrastructure (2026): 'New Zealand... can borrow carefully'; 'New Zealand's balance sheet is strong'; raise up to $60b for infrastructure; health to 9% of GDP. Spending on investment prioritised over debt reduction; qualified.

alliance.evidence: Coder A: Alliance: large tax-funded expansion of free health, universal benefits, state housing and public job creation (Tax Justice and costings documents, Sep 2026); no debt-reduction priority stated. conservative.evidence: Coder A: Conservatives 'committed to urgently tackling the massive debt'; cut hospital waiting times funded from bureaucracy and productivity savings, 'the key issue is whether patients are treated in time, not how much is spent'. statements.text: People who commit serious crimes should be given longer prison sentences, even if it means more people in prison for longer at public expense.

national.evidence: Coder A: National restored Three Strikes (Act passed 13 Dec 2024), capped sentence discounts at 40% (Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Act, Mar 2025), and campaigns on 'Capping sentence discounts... Restoring Three Strikes for the worst repeat offenders' and tougher sentences for sexual offending (2026). Coder B: Voted for Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Act (3rd reading 13 Dec 2024) and sentencing-discount caps; campaign launch 27 Sep 2026: 'locking offenders up for longer to keep our community safe'; 240 extra prison beds at Christchurch Men's Prison.

labour.evidence: Coder A: Labour voted against the Reinstating Three Strikes Bill (all readings, 2024) and the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill (Mar 2025); Webb: minimum sentencing laws 'do little to reduce serious crime'. Hipkins would not confirm repeal, so opposition is qualified. Coder B: Voted against Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Act (Dec 2024; Duncan Webb: minimum-sentence laws 'did little to reduce serious crime'); no 2026 pledge to repeal.

green.evidence: Manifesto 2026 (Justice): 'Enable judicial discretion in sentencing, including by abolishing mandatory minimum sentences, life sentences, preventive detention, limits on sentence discounts, three strikes'; prioritise rehabilitation.
